paras: The attempted lynching in Gonzales County, Texas, was the pursuit in late September 1882 of an unnamed Black prisoner, charged with assaulting a 12-year-old girl near Gonzales, by a mob reported at about 250 men. Officers moved him from jail to jail and finally by night and rail to San Antonio, where he was lodged safely in jail. The Dallas Herald told the story as a 'thrilling game of hide-and-seek' won by a state Ranger, Sergeant Rudd.

The man, described only as 'a negro', was charged with 'outraging the person of a 12-year-old girl' about six miles east of Gonzales. He was captured and jailed at Cuero, in De Witt County, and according to the report a mob was organized 'for the purpose of meting out summary justice' as soon as word of his capture spread.

When Cuero officials heard of the mob, they sent the prisoner to the Victoria jail, but after a day or so word came that a mob was coming there, and he was returned to Cuero. Judging that they would either have to give him up or cause 'great bloodshed', the Cuero officials turned him over to Sergeant Rudd of Captain Oglesby's command of state troops.

Rudd, with Deputy Sheriff Kilgore of De Witt County, took the prisoner at night to Gonzales and then to Harwood, where he boarded the early train to Waelder, giving the impression that he was bound for Houston. Instead he returned on the next westbound train, passed through Harwood, where a branch of the mob was waiting, and went on to San Antonio, lodging the prisoner in the jail there. The informant said the mob numbered about 250 and that 'the entire county of Gonzales seemed anxious to get hold of the negro.'

Rudd was quoted as saying he would like to see the prisoner punished but that it was his duty to protect him 'that the law might take its course.' The coverage does not name the accused or report an indictment, trial or verdict, and no arrests of mob members were reported.

The only account found was a special dated San Antonio, September 29, based on what 'a gentleman, who is just up from Gonzales' told a reporter, which ran on the front page of the Dallas Daily Herald on September 30 and again, verbatim, in the Dallas Weekly Herald on October 5. Its headline cast the episode as a contest that Rudd 'Plays' with 'a Determined Mob And Wins', and the text praised the officer's 'determination, self-sacrifice, and ultimate success' as 'almost without paralel.' At the same time the paper treated the charge as proven, calling the prisoner a 'negro fiend' and 'the villain', and closed by remarking without comment that he 'would probably have been burned at the stake.'
No other paper's version, local Gonzales or Cuero report, or Black-press account appears in the coverage.

reader.title: Attempted lynching in Gonzales County, Texas (1882)
bases: A mob of about 250 organized to seize and kill a Black prisoner accused of rape and hunted him while officers moved him from jail to jail; no one was killed (A1).

The mob of about 250 sought 'summary justice' for an alleged rape, but officers kept the prisoner from it and lodged him in the San Antonio jail, so no one was killed; it was an attempted lynching (A1).
Only one report, a San Antonio special to the Dallas Herald based on an unnamed informant and the officer's statement, was found; the weekly edition reprinted it verbatim (A1, A2).

info: Late September 1882; the report was dated San Antonio, September 29, and the earlier transfers are not dated
Alleged crime about six miles east of Gonzales; prisoner held at Cuero and Victoria, moved through Gonzales, Harwood and Waelder to San Antonio; a branch of the mob waited at Harwood
One unnamed Black man ('a negro'), the prisoner the mob sought; not harmed
Charged with 'outraging the person of a 12-year-old girl' about six miles east of Gonzales

sources.note: San Antonio special of Sept. 29 from an unnamed gentleman from Gonzales: an unnamed Black prisoner moved from Cuero to Victoria, back to Cuero, then by Sergeant Rudd via Gonzales, Harwood and Waelder to San Antonio jail ahead of a mob of about 250.

The entire county of Gonzales seemed anxious to get hold of the negro, and the mob hunting him numbered about 250.
